title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
description: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gamblin
body: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work.This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items.The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable".A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms."Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year.Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair"."The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said."Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided"."Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said."We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

schema.headline: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes

title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
description: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vuln
body: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair."I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day. "I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting."I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened."I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her."I'm learning that things can get better," she said."I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health."Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids."I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had  a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics."The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said."The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives."We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear."We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death."Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life."I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023."He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said."Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness."Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living."That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him."When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis."Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said."The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart."It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."The hearing continues.If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair

title: 'Proteinflation': Meet the people paying up to £100 for a bag of protein
description: There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust.Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past cou
body: There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust.Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago.For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max."It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says."If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly."But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story."It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says.Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag.

schema.headline: 'Proteinflation': Meet the people paying up to £100 for a bag of protein

title: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
description: The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it
body: The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination.Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face.Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity. However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation.Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures"."International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added.Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks.Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector."We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month.Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday. "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman.He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology".He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes"."We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added.Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches.  Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole".He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety".    "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added. "But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale."Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure."All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology.Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI. Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia. The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

schema.headline: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards

title: Michael Kiwanuka: Singer reveals he is recovering from a stroke
description: Image caption, Kiwanuka said he has had "a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAward
body: Image caption, Kiwanuka said he has had "a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAward-winning singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has revealed he has suffered a stroke and faces a "long, tough journey ahead" to recover.The 39-year-old from London, who won the Mercury Prize in 2020 and has been nominated for five Brit Awards, said in an Instagram post that the stroke occurred "a few months ago" and was caused "by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure".He added that "the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done", but told fans he will "look forward to seeing you all soon".Kiwanuka simultaneously announced the release of his fifth album, titled Fudge, which was recorded before the stroke.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kiwanuka performed on Glastonbury Festival's Pyramid Stage in 2024"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said."I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure."It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon."I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better."It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."'One of the toughest challenges'He thanked "all the incredible NHS staff and every single medical professional who has helped care for me and continue to help and encourage me in my recovery", and his friends and family for their support."This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I've faced and I'll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road."Fans and fellow artists sent well wishes, with BBC Radio 6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne replying: "So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx."US singer Miguel wrote: "Man, take your time healing, you are needed brother."Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien posted: "Sending love to you Michael."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kiwanuka won the Mercury Prize for his self-titled third album in 2020Kiwanuka first made his mark 15 years ago, being named the BBC's Sound of 2012, and has established himself as one of Britain's most acclaimed singers and songwriters.His first three albums were nominated for the prestigious Mercury Prize for best British or Irish album of the year. He won the trophy in 2020 with his third record, Kiwanuka.That album also earned him nominations for best male solo artist and album of the year at the Brits, and best rock album at the Grammy Awards.He is also known for the song Cold Little Heart, which was used as the theme tune for US TV drama Big Little Lies. But in July 2025 he cancelled all live shows on medical advice because of what was described as "continued illness".Fudge was originally scheduled to come out last year. Before it was postponed, an early review in Mojo Magazine described it as an "intimate" and "brooding" album, influence by Neil Young's On The Beach.

schema.headline: Michael Kiwanuka: Singer reveals he is recovering from a stroke

title: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
description: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide du
body: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran. The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew". He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time". Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions,  calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable". "What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday."Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US. US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageUS sailors arrive in Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at seaSuicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.A study, external of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

schema.headline: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says

title: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
description: Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".The prime minist
body: Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton. Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. "And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis. "But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. "It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

schema.headline: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'

title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
description: The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been tol
body: The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy £1.4bn a day."Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said."We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said the threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week". The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites. Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space. However, Washington has already accused both Russia and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.In May, the RAF tracked a series of "dangerous manoeuvres" by five Russian satellites moving close to two Finnish commercial satellites. The RAF's Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said in June that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across Europe and Canada.The UK has a handful of military satellites in orbit for surveillance and military communications. But it works closely with the US Space Force - which has many more.In a separate speech at the space conference, ACM Smyth added that "unfortunately we are seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries".ACM Smyth warned that without satellites, some of the technologies people take for granted would be lost and would make every sector "less efficient, less prosperous and less secure"."Sat-nav systems would fail, congestion on our roads would be severe and our emergency services would take longer to help those in need," he said, adding that satellites are also needed to monitor the weather and the effects of climate change.

schema.headline: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told

title: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
description: Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBCImage caption, Residents like Sam told the BBC they were shocked by their blood test resultsByEsme Stallard, Tom Ingham
body: Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBCImage caption, Residents like Sam told the BBC they were shocked by their blood test resultsByEsme Stallard, Tom Ingham and Jonah FisherClimate and science teamBlood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result."When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale. "I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.'It's quite emotional, a shock'Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear.But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer.The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated.They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens.Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air.Image caption, Two allotments in Thornton-Cleveleys have been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated landResidents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals".Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues.Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday.Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category."I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't."Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family."One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said.Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick."To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBCImage caption, Andrew Molloy expected his results would be normalThe UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do.Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines.Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis.Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening.Factory to close later this yearMore than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contaminationSarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally".The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country.Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing.The factory in Thornton-Cleveleys first start operating in the 1950s, when ICI manufactured coating for non-stick frying pans using PFOA. AGC Chemicals took over the factory in 1999 and continued using PFOA until 2012, when it switched to a replacement chemical called EEA-NH4, which was also found in the blood of 10 residents tested.A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals said the site manufactured chemicals long before the company was established. "Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps," they said.Earlier this month, AGC Chemicals said the factory would close later this year after deciding there was no "viable solution to keep the site operating in the context of a volatile and competitive market".Dr Steve Hajioff, a specialist in public health, who was not involved in the Thornton-Cleveleys blood testing, said PFOA levels could have been even higher in the past, given the factory stopped using the substance in 2012 and it does break down over time.He said the levels measured in Thornton-Cleveleys are associated with elevated risks of serious health condition, but added: "If you increase the risk of something really rare, like kidney cancer or testicular cancer, by 30%, then the chances of an individual getting affected are still pretty low."Moore said she was representing residents in the community who were pregnant and worried about their children, as well as those who have families who were refusing to visit their homes over concerns about the risks."What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning," she added.The researchers said further blood testing should be done in the wider community to understand the scale of the issue.A previous report into PFAS in Jersey recommended that residents with elevated levels should be offered treatment, including cholesterol-lowering medications and blood letting - a treatment where blood is gradually withdrawn from a vein, allowing the body to naturally replenish it.Wyre Borough Council, which is overseeing the investigation into the site, said: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available."The Truth About Forever ChemicalsReporter Catrin Nye reveals how PFAS can affect health and contaminate the environment, and she asks if the UK government is doing enough to keep us safe.Watch on iPlayer now or on BBC One on Monday 1 December at 20:00 GMT (20:30 in Northern Ireland, 23:15 in Scotland)

schema.headline: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory

title: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia
description: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating
body: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new wordBySmitha MundasadHealth reporter Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental."Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame"."It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.'Sex positivity'Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.Image source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame."Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.'Virginity membrane'Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once."With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".Image source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."'Judgmental words'Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first."Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue."Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected."Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress."I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

schema.headline: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium
description: Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has s
body: Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for the team's new stadium.Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, the club have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.However, while United have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, net finance costs alone have now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club have not explained what they have done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximately 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first-team squad this summer.United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than promoted Ipswich.However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches because of injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts."We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada."This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years."While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, who currently sit second bottom of the table with one point from three games.Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m."This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first-team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

schema.headline: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: 1,000-goal target and Portugal ambition fuel football icon
description: Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to fur
body: Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals.The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain.However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night.In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark.Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did."Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think."The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want."I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football."Ronaldo is a two-time Nations League winner with Portugal, and he said adding a third title was also an aim alongside his personal ambitions."Both aims are important," he said."One thousand goals, yes, and the national team. Winning the Nations League, the competition starts tomorrow [Thursday], it's a new age."Young talents including Fabio Silva, Renato Veiga, Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves and Francisco Conceicao all feature in Portugal's squad for this international window.Ronaldo - who joked he will play on for another decade - says helping his country's newest talents was also a pivotal factor in his decision to continue to represent Portugal."This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games," he said."For me, the most important thing, I know what I am. I know what I do to be here, to have the success that I have."I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired... in 10 years!"I'm happy with myself. It doesn't matter if I play tomorrow, if I rest the next game. For me, the most important thing is that I feel good."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo: 1,000-goal target and Portugal ambition fuel football icon

title: Dopamine sites: India and the world are discovering the thrill of shopping without buying
description: Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'ByIndia correspondentYou are hungry. Or you are not. It do
body: Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'ByIndia correspondentYou are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen."Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June. It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience. Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel. What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily needWhat begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared."Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025 Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience"."Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction."To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway.What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'". But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve. "While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh BachchanBut there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace. Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate"."The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset."I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go'The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain"."In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

schema.headline: Dopamine sites: India and the world are discovering the thrill of shopping without buying

title: Home Secretary hits out at 'unacceptable' migrant landings in Kent
description: Figure caption, Watch: Migrant boat arrives on beach near FolkestoneByDaniel SandfordUK correspondentSimon Jonesin Dover and Tanya GuptaSouth EastThe
body: Figure caption, Watch: Migrant boat arrives on beach near FolkestoneByDaniel SandfordUK correspondentSimon Jonesin Dover and Tanya GuptaSouth EastThe Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.  Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.'Gangs using new tactics'Migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats.Before Monday, no small boats had been officially recorded as arriving in the UK without an escort since 6 September 2025.Uncontrolled landings of migrants in the UK, as seen on Monday and Tuesday, are so rare that the incident in 2025 was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The home secretary has ordered an urgent review after the landingsMahmood said the beach landings were "not acceptable".She said: "Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many."That is why I have ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command into how this happened, and what must be done to ensure it doesn't happen again."She said that new tactics adopted by people smugglers, including launching small boats from much further west in France, were "a reminder of two things".The home secretary said: "Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings."Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat."Early on Wednesday, migrants were brought to Dover after embarking on a crossing from a village near Bayeux in Normandy to Gosport in Hampshire, spending more than 33 hours at sea.Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, called it "a day of despair" for the Labour government.He said: "Our border security has descended into chaos with illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats."Philp said: "This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants' boats in French waters, instead they are escorting them here.""What's more, there have been two uncontrolled migrant landings in a week. It is a complete free for all – the Labour government have no idea who is coming into the country."The only way to stop Channel crossings is to deport anyone who arrives illegally to their home country or a safe third country. That's the only way we can end this madness."Image source, SWNSImage caption, A boat came ashore near Folkestone in one of two uncontrolled landings in two daysEarlier, a government spokesperson said: "Border Security Command officers alongside Kent Police have been responding to an incident in Dover."Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response."There is a thorough investigation ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."Officials said those who had been detained had been taken to Western Jet Foil for processing.The uncontrolled arrivals come after Border Security Command suggested they were a thing of the past, because of new surveillance technology and improved resources.Earlier this year, Reform UK set out a proposal to call in the Royal Navy to help intercept migrants, but it was rejected.On Tuesday, 154 migrants arrived in three boats, of which one was an uncontrolled landing.It takes the total of migrants to have arrived in the UK this year to 17,784.The total so far this year is down 44.7% compared with figures for 22 September 2025, at which point 32,188 migrants had arrived that year.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external,  X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Home Secretary hits out at 'unacceptable' migrant landings in Kent

title: Swansea woman's migraines dismissed by GP as 'dramatic'
description: Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb
body: Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb numbness, ability to walk and carry out a journey, brain fog, sleep, neck pain, mood swings, visual aura, sound sensitivity, cravings, vertigo."I would wake up daily either in pain or worried about when it would start."She also spent a huge amount of time researching triggers and spent "hundreds on various things just to see if that would help" - from vitamins to chiropractors.Lauren was training to become a biomedical scientist in the NHS but the lights and overstimulation of Singleton Hospital were so intense she had daily migraines. She added that she often felt dismissed by colleagues who implied she was faking her condition but was lucky that her manager was supportive.Some colleagues would accommodate her by turning off the lights, she said, but others said: "If you don't get your annual leave approved, you can just say you've got a migraine and you won't come in."That was so untrue. So you're battling, not just your physical health. You're battling all the mental side that comes with it as well."If I went home every day at the sight of a migraine, I would never be in work. There wasn't a day without pain and if there was, I'd be waiting for it."To manage her symptoms, Lauren changed her working hours, starting at 08:00 BST and finishing at 16:00 so she could get home to take medication, but was still "in agony". "I couldn't make plans because I knew I'd be suffering in the evening. My weekends would basically be spent recovering," she said.Lauren saw a crisis team in December, was signed off work for a month and her migraine attacks began to ease.She decided it was time to leave her biomedical scientist career and now has a job at an insurance firm, and feels like a different person."I have never done so many hobbies in my life," she said."Jewellery making, painting... and running 50k in September for a charity."Her new medication is working well, but she added: "If it got bad again, I honestly wouldn't know where to turn to."Swansea Bay health board said it was "very sorry to hear of the patient's concerns" but could not comment on individual cases without consent and "would welcome the patient getting in touch with us so we can discuss this further". It said it had a "specialist headache clinic that covers conditions such as migraine, which GPs can refer people to when appropriate".Munro said headaches were a symptom of migraine attacks, but so too are "visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting, sometimes numbness and tingling, sometimes abdominal pain, sometimes dizziness". They are also a spectrum condition, she said, from episodic - meaning people have mild or rare attacks - to chronic where they have more than 15 days a month affected by migraine symptoms. "If you have a migraine attack and you put up with it and then you have another one and put up with it, your brain actually gets more irritable," she said.That means the migraines become more regular and can become chronic if effective treatment is not applied.The first barrier to treatment, Munro said, is that a lot of people believe they are "normal headaches".She said people should always get repetitive headaches checked out by a GP.The next barrier is that GPs often just note down the headaches as a symptom rather than diagnose migraine. The third barrier is the medication that was offered in the past, though this has improved in the last five years, she said."We need better education throughout the whole of society about how significant migraine is to people who suffer from it."The Welsh government said it recognised the effect migraines can have on people's lives and that guidance was available to help NHS staff diagnose and manage conditions.The UK government said National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had "clear guidance on the diagnosis and management of migraines, and we expect healthcare professionals to follow it and deliver high-quality care to all patients".If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Swansea woman's migraines dismissed by GP as 'dramatic'
